comment: Memory-API inventory for the memory-safety overlay passes. One entry per API,
recording the ROLE of each argument so a consumer writes tag lookups instead of
hard-coded argument indices. Sources: POSIX Issue 7, Linux man-pages (malloc(3),
memcpy(3), read(2), ...), and the usage of these APIs in real C code bases such as FFmpeg.
Deliberately omitted: wide-char and _s variants (wcscpy, memcpy_s, ...) and Win32 APIs
(alloca is included, as the `stack` family). They surface in
the coverage report as 'seen but not inventoried', which is how this list is meant to
grow - an entry here needs its man-page argument roles, nothing else.
Argument indices are 1-based. `untrustedCall` marks a call whose RESULT or variadic
outputs carry untrusted data with no single buffer argument to point at (getenv, the
scanf family). C++ new/delete are indistinguishable from new[]/delete[] in the graph
(the frontend emits the same operator for both), so both carry the plain `new` family.
Count-by-size allocators (calloc, reallocarray) declare both factors: `count` is the
element-count role and `len` the byte-size role; both arguments carry the mem-len tag
and the overflow question is asked about the product. A realloc is the
third family, `realloc`: it invalidates its input pointer and returns a fresh
allocation, so it carries neither the alloc nor the free tag.

Clamp entries: the value records what the call establishes about its result - min (bounded above by each argument), max (bounded below), clip (arg2 below, arg3 above). FFMIN/FFMAX/av_clip are FFmpeg's clamping macros; a project's own MYMIN is an external-config entry in the same shape. Used by GuardPass for clamps the frontend left unexpanded.
Nullable-return entries: `nullableReturn` marks an API whose result may be NULL -
allocation-family calls that return POINTERS declare it explicitly; the fd-returning family
(open, socket, accept) does NOT: an int fd's failure is -1, checked with `< 0`, and conflating
the two would turn a checked fd into a null-deref finding. Neither does mmap, which fails with
MAP_FAILED ((void *) -1), not NULL: its correct check is no null guard. The pass emits `nullable-return` on the
call for MS-NULL-001: a dereference of the result with no narrowing guard between call and use.
Descriptor families: every int descriptor is one `fd` family - open, openat, creat, socket,
accept, accept4, dup and dup2 hand out the same kind of handle, and close releases it;
closesocket (declared in winsock2.h) is that release's Windows spelling, the one Winsock
entry beside the POSIX names. `FILE *` and `DIR` streams keep the `file` family (fopen,
fdopen, freopen, tmpfile, opendir; released by fclose and closedir), so close() of a stream
and fclose of a descriptor are family mismatches while close() of a socket is a correct
pairing - a separate socket family reported exactly that pairing as a mismatch.
The str*-search family reads through its HAYSTACK, which is argument 1 (`src: 1`), not the
needle/char, so passing a pointer to be searched counts as a read-through; `strlen` is a
reader of the same shape. These are the entries that decide whether handing a possibly-null
pointer to a call is a dereference.
FORTIFY and builtin spellings: a `__builtin_X` call is the API X itself (same arguments), which the
loader derives for every entry. The `_chk` wrappers the C library's _FORTIFY_SOURCE turns calls
into (`__memcpy_chk`, and the compiler's `__builtin___memcpy_chk`) take an extra argument, the
destination size the compiler worked out, and some move their other arguments: each has its own
entry, with `api` naming the API its tags are valued with and `objectSize` that argument.

`untrustedPrefixes` names the input functions of verification benchmarks by prefix: SV-COMP's `__VERIFIER_nondet_int` and CBMC's `nondet_*` return any value - the program's input - so their results are untrusted like getenv's.

The readers that fill a caller's buffer (read, recv, fgets, fread, ...) declare it as `dst` beside `untrustedRead`: the bytes they write are bounded by their length argument, which the destination must hold (CBMC's library models assert `w_ok(buf, n)`).

Profiles: a library profile declares the memory management of a translation unit that includes one of its headers, matched by basename. Entries use the shape above plus roles nothing in an analysed tree can confirm, because the declarations sit in headers outside the input: `release`, `acquire`, `steal` and `retains` (1-based parameter indices; `retains` names the argument whose resource the result takes over, as fdopen takes its descriptor), `cleanup` (the call frees the pointee of a pointer-to-pointer argument), `region` (`{"role": "create"}` when the call's result is a new region, `{"role": "create", "arg": <index>}` when the created region is stored through an out-pointer argument, `{"role": "allocate", "arg": <index>}` when the region is an argument, `{"role": "allocate", "context": "<global>"}` when it is a named global, `{"role": "reset" | "destroy", "arg": <index>}` for calls that empty or tear down their region argument), and `source`, naming the header or documentation page that states the behaviour. Families say which releases are interchangeable: the kernel's `slab`, `vmalloc` and `kvmalloc` families are released by kfree, vfree and kvfree respectively, and kvfree's `free` lists all three because it accepts each, and each pool, context or request library gets a family of its own (`pgmem`, `aprpool`, `ngxpool`, `pymem`, `zendmm`); glib's allocators and nginx's malloc wrappers sit on the heap family because their frees are free() on the platforms in question, g_free since GLib 2.46 and ngx_free by its define. A malformed role drops its entry with a note on stderr.

apis.name: tmpfile
apis.source: stdio's tmpfile(3), POSIX and Linux man-pages: creates a temporary file opened for update, removed on close; returns NULL when no file could be created

apis.name: creat
apis.source: creat(2), POSIX and Linux man-pages: equivalent to open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, mode); returns a descriptor or -1

apis.name: dup
apis.source: dup(2), POSIX and Linux man-pages: returns a new descriptor referring to the same open file description as oldfd, or -1

apis.name: dup2
apis.source: dup2(2), POSIX and Linux man-pages: makes oldfd's copy on newfd and returns newfd, or -1

apis.name: closesocket
apis.source: closesocket is declared in winsock2.h (Winsock2, https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-closesocket): closes a socket descriptor, the Windows spelling of close

apis.name: accept4
apis.source: accept4(2), Linux man-pages: accept with a flags argument; returns a descriptor or -1 and fills the peer address buffer like accept

entries.name: g_new0
entries.source: glib/gmem.h (g_new0); https://docs.gtk.org/glib/func.new0.html: allocates n_structs zeroed elements of struct_type, so the size is the product of the element size and argument 2

entries.name: g_free
entries.source: glib/gmem.h (g_free); https://docs.gtk.org/glib/memory.html: since GLib 2.46 g_malloc is hardcoded to the system malloc implementation, so g_free is free() on every platform GLib supports

entries.name: g_steal_pointer
entries.source: glib/gmem.h (g_steal_pointer); https://docs.gtk.org/glib/func.steal_pointer.html: sets pp to NULL, returning the value that was there before

entries.name: g_autoptr_cleanup_generic_gfree
entries.source: glib/glib-autocleanups.h (g_autoptr_cleanup_generic_gfree): the cleanup g_autofree attaches, which calls g_free on the pointer its argument points to

entries.name: kmalloc
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kmalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: the normal way to allocate from the slab allocator, returns NULL when the request fails

entries.name: kzalloc
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kzalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: allocates from the slab allocator like kmalloc and the memory is set to zero

entries.name: vmalloc
entries.source: linux/vmalloc.h (vmalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: allocates virtually contiguous memory of the requested size, returns NULL when the request cannot be satisfied

entries.name: kcalloc
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kcalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: allocates memory for an array of argument 1 elements of argument 2 bytes from the slab allocator, set to zero

entries.name: kmalloc_array
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kmalloc_array); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: allocates memory for an array of argument 1 elements of argument 2 bytes from the slab allocator

entries.name: kvmalloc
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kvmalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: tries kmalloc and falls back to vmalloc, so the memory must be freed with kvfree

entries.name: kvzalloc
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kvzalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: kvmalloc with the memory set to zero, freed with kvfree

entries.name: kfree
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kfree); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: frees memory allocated with kmalloc; it must not be given vmalloc memory

entries.name: vfree
entries.source: linux/vmalloc.h (vfree); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/mm-api.html: releases memory allocated by vmalloc

entries.name: kvfree
entries.source: linux/slab.h (kvfree declaration); mm/slub.c kvfree() kerneldoc: frees memory allocated by any of vmalloc(), kmalloc() or kvmalloc()

entries.name: devm_kzalloc
entries.source: linux/device.h (devm_kzalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/driver-model/devres.html and devm_kzalloc(9): managed kzalloc whose memory is freed automatically on driver detach, owned by the dev argument 1

entries.name: devm_kcalloc
entries.source: linux/device.h (devm_kcalloc); https://docs.kernel.org/driver-api/driver-model/devres.html: managed array allocation owned by the dev argument 1, counting argument 2 elements of the size in argument 3

entries.name: kref_put
entries.source: linux/kref.h (kref_put); https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/kref.html: decrements the refcount of argument 1 and calls the release callback, which is argument 2, when it reaches zero

entries.name: palloc
entries.source: postgres.h and utils/palloc.h (palloc, CurrentMemoryContext); https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/spi-memory.html: allocates from the current memory context, the CurrentMemoryContext global

entries.name: palloc0
entries.source: utils/palloc.h (palloc0); https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/spi-memory.html: allocates zeroed memory from the current memory context

entries.name: pfree
entries.source: utils/palloc.h (pfree); src/backend/utils/mmgr/README (https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/utils/mmgr/README): frees memory allocated with palloc

entries.name: MemoryContextReset
entries.source: utils/memutils.h (MemoryContextReset); src/backend/utils/mmgr/README: reset frees all memory allocated in the context, the context itself stays valid

entries.name: MemoryContextDelete
entries.source: utils/memutils.h (MemoryContextDelete); src/backend/utils/mmgr/README: delete frees the context's memory and destroys the context itself and its children

entries.name: AllocSetContextCreate
entries.source: utils/memutils.h (AllocSetContextCreate); src/backend/utils/mmgr/README: creates a new allocator-set context, the call's result is the new region

entries.name: apr_palloc
entries.source: apr_pools.h (apr_palloc); https://apr.apache.org/docs/apr/trunk/group__apr__pools.html: allocates size bytes from pool p, the pool is argument 1

entries.name: apr_pool_create
entries.source: apr_pools.h (apr_pool_create); https://apr.apache.org/docs/apr/trunk/group__apr__pools.html: creates a new pool and hands it out through the first argument, an out-pointer, returning a status code

entries.name: apr_pool_clear
entries.source: apr_pools.h (apr_pool_clear); https://apr.apache.org/docs/apr/trunk/group__apr__pools.html: frees all memory in the pool, keeping the pool itself for reuse

entries.name: apr_pool_destroy
entries.source: apr_pools.h (apr_pool_destroy); https://apr.apache.org/docs/apr/trunk/group__apr__pools.html: destroys the pool and everything allocated from it

entries.name: ngx_alloc
entries.source: src/os/unix/ngx_alloc.h (ngx_alloc); nginx development guide https://nginx.org/en/docs/dev/development_guide.html: wrapper around malloc() with logging, returns NULL when malloc fails

entries.name: ngx_free
entries.source: src/os/unix/ngx_alloc.h (ngx_free is defined as free); nginx development guide: wrapper around free() for memory ngx_alloc returned

entries.name: ngx_palloc
entries.source: src/core/ngx_palloc.h (ngx_palloc); nginx development guide: allocates aligned memory from the pool given as argument 1

entries.name: ngx_create_pool
entries.source: src/core/ngx_palloc.h (ngx_create_pool); nginx development guide: creates a pool with the specified block size

entries.name: ngx_destroy_pool
entries.source: src/core/ngx_palloc.h (ngx_destroy_pool); nginx development guide: frees all pool memory, including the pool object itself

entries.name: PyMem_Malloc
entries.source: Include/pymem.h (PyMem_Malloc); https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/memory.html: allocates n bytes from the pymem domain and returns NULL on error; the result must be freed with PyMem_Free

entries.name: PyMem_Free
entries.source: Include/pymem.h (PyMem_Free); https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/memory.html: frees memory allocated by PyMem_Malloc

entries.name: Py_DECREF
entries.source: Include/object.h (Py_DECREF); https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/refcounting.html: decrements the reference count of the object given as argument 1 and calls its deallocator when it reaches zero

entries.name: Py_INCREF
entries.source: Include/object.h (Py_INCREF); https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/refcounting.html: increments the reference count of the object given as argument 1

entries.name: emalloc
entries.source: Zend/zend_alloc.h (emalloc); https://www.phpinternalsbook.com/php7/memory_management/zend_memory_manager.html: allocates from the request heap the Zend memory manager owns, the memory is released back to it at request end

entries.name: efree
entries.source: Zend/zend_alloc.h (efree); https://www.phpinternalsbook.com/php7/memory_management/zend_memory_manager.html: frees a block emalloc allocated from the Zend memory manager's request heap

entries.name: zend_string_release
entries.source: Zend/zend_string.h (zend_string_release); https://www.phpinternalsbook.com/php7/internal_types/strings/zend_strings.html: decrements the string's refcount and frees it when the count drops to zero
